description:
Miss the target. Keep the mission.

Landers miss their targets by hundreds of meters, and launches slip by weeks. We're building MARGEN, a tool that tests a Moon landing plan against those errors before launch, using NASA data.
summary:
MARGEN is a web app to check if a Moon landing plan still works when things don't go as planned. Landers miss their target by hundreds of meters and launches get delayed, and at the lunar south pole that can be enough to lose sunlight or contact with Earth.

You pick a site, a date and an aim point. MARGEN simulates 1,000 landings around that point and checks each one for flat ground, sunlight and Earth in view, on landing day and over the next two weeks. It tells you how many work, why the rest fail, where the safest spot is, how many days of delay the plan can take, and the next date that works. There are eleven south-pole sites, including Athena's target on Mons Mouton and the nine Artemis III candidate regions.

It uses NASA LRO LOLA terrain and JPL ephemerides, and we compared it against NASA's illumination maps and JPL Horizons. It runs in the browser at margen.vip.
details:
What it does

MARGEN answers one question for a landing at the lunar south pole: if the lander misses its target or the launch slips, does the mission still work?

You choose one of eleven sites (the Shackleton connecting ridge, Athena's target on Mons Mouton, and one site in each of the nine Artemis III candidate regions), a landing date in 2027 and an aim point on a 2 x 2 km terrain map. MARGEN scatters 1,000 simulated landings around the aim, with a 100 m typical miss, and checks each one. A landing works if the ground slopes 10 degrees or less, the Sun is up at least half of the first day and of the first 14 days, and Earth is in view at least 30% of that time.

The app shows how many landings work, why the others fail (too steep, not enough sunlight, or Earth out of view), how many days late the launch can be, and the next date that works with the same aim. "Aim at the safest spot" moves the aim to the best nearby point. A table compares the eleven sites on the chosen date, and a horizon view shows the Sun and Earth moving over the real terrain for the first two weeks, so you can see when they drop behind the hills. Any view can be shared with a link.

How it works

A Python pipeline traces the horizon in 360 directions for every 20 m spot of each site, using NASA LRO LOLA terrain (20 m near the site, 80 m out to 250 km) and the Moon's curvature. Sun and Earth positions for every hour of 2027 come from JPL DE440 through NAIF SPICE. The browser does the rest: slope, the 1,000 landings and the checks. There is no server; it is a static site.

Validation

We wrote the pass marks before measuring. Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.00003 degrees. Across 160 random spots near the pole, sunlight differs from NASA's AVGVISIB maps by 1.75 points on average (r = 0.985) and Earth in view by 1.16 points (r = 0.982). On the day Athena landed, MARGEN puts the Sun 2.464 degrees above the horizon, the same as JPL Horizons. Two checks missed: the 1,000-landing estimate can vary by up to 3.1 points (the goal was 3), and at the landing sites MARGEN finds about 5 points less sunlight than NASA's map, so its chances lean cautious. All of this is on margen.vip/validation.html, along with what the model leaves out: rocks and craters smaller than 20 m, batteries, temperature and radio links.

Why it matters

Many of the next lunar landers are headed to the south pole, where a few hundred meters or a few days can decide whether a lander gets power and can talk to Earth. MARGEN lets mission planners, teachers and anyone curious test a plan against both kinds of error and find safer options before launch. It is free and open source (Apache-2.0).

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy, tifffile, fsspec), TypeScript with Vite and Canvas 2D, and Remotion for the demo video. Code: https://github.com/spexeyy/margen
